source: The SWE Glow-Up handbook, user supplied, research snapshot November 4 2026

skills.text: Name all eight primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.
Know integral widths and when to choose int vs long; learn overflow and underflow examples.
Distinguish a char (single UTF-16 code unit) from a String (object of text).
Know float vs double literals; 3.14 is double, 3.14f is float.
Know numeric promotions: byte/short/char arithmetic generally promotes to int.
Explain implicit widening versus explicit narrowing casts; know possible loss of information.
Understand integer division: 7/2 = 3, while 7.0/2 = 3.5.
Explain modulo, negative remainder behavior, and extracting decimal digits.
Know primitive array defaults: numeric 0, char '\u0000', boolean false.
Know null is a reference value, not a legal int/boolean primitive value.
Declare, initialize, reassign, and distinguish local variable scope from instance fields.
Use +, -, *, /, %, +=, -= and distinguish prefix ++i and postfix i++.
Use ==, !=, <=, >=, &&, ||, ! with short-circuit evaluation.
Know operator precedence; explicitly add parentheses in tricky conditions.
Recognize Math.max, Math.min, Math.abs, Math.pow and when int overflow matters.
Explain why String + int concatenates rather than adds; force numeric addition first.
Use Integer.MAX_VALUE / MIN_VALUE; know the issue with Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE).
Write if/else-if/else including nested conditions and boolean expressions.
Use switch expressions/statement cautiously; explain break and fall-through in older switch statements.
Declare a method, distinguish return type, parameters, arguments and method calls.
Know public/private/static at an introductory level; understand main signature.
Understand pass-by-value: Java passes copies of primitive values and reference values.
Explain a local variable's lifetime, block scope, and definite assignment.
Recognize method overloading vs overriding (preview only).
Write for (init; condition; update), explaining every clause.
Use i < a.length rather than i <= a.length; explain valid indices.
Understand for-each loops and why modifying loop variable does not replace primitive array elements.
Write while loops when number of iterations is unknown; ensure the condition changes.
Know do-while executes at least once; recognize when it is useful.
Use continue vs break correctly without accidentally skipping required updates.
Trace nested loops and identify row and column index separately.
Prove termination and find off-by-one errors on tiny inputs.
Identify ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NullPointerException, NumberFormatException.
Distinguish compile errors from runtime errors from logical bugs.
Test zero-length, one-element, duplicates, all negatives, all positives, and maximum input size as relevant.
Use assert/println while learning, and remove debugging noise from final solutions.
Declare int[] a; initialize int[] a = {2, 4, 6}; allocate new int[3].
Explain a.length (property) vs String.length() and List.size() (methods).
Read a[0], a[i], a[a.length-1]; write a[i] = newValue.
Know array size stays fixed but element values can change.
Understand arrays of primitives vs reference slots, including default null.
Trace aliases: int[] b = a; b[0] = 7 also modifies a[0].
Explain new output array versus modifying input in place.
Know Arrays.toString for display; printing a raw array does not display elements.
Understand shallow copy for object arrays and top-level clone of primitive arrays.
Use enhanced-for for reading values; indexed loop when writing to positions.
Understand int[][] means an outer array whose elements refer to int[] row arrays.
Draw 2 rows and 3 columns for int[][] g = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6}}.
Know g.length = number of row slots; g[i].length = length of selected row.
Access g[i][j] and traverse all cells safely with nested loops.
Distinguish 2D rectangular from jagged: {{1},{2,3,4}}.
Explain new int[3][] leaves all row references null until rows allocated.
Learn row-major traversal and when column-major traversal needs rectangularity checks.
Know 2D new int[m][n] initializes integer cells to zero.
Know Arrays.deepToString for displaying nested arrays.
Distinguish clone() on int[][] from copying each int[] row separately.
Compute running sum and maximum/minimum; seed max with a[0] on nonempty input.
Count values matching a predicate without overwriting count accidentally.
Use Arrays.toString(a) for 1D display; Arrays.deepToString(matrix) for nested.
Explain Arrays.fill(a,value) overwrites every slot; overload for a range.
Know Arrays.copyOf(a,newLength): new top-level array; truncation/padding behavior.
Know Arrays.copyOfRange(a,from,to): from inclusive, to exclusive; padding when allowed.
Use System.arraycopy(src,srcPos,dst,dstPos,count) safely; destination already exists.
Understand a.clone() produces a new top-level array and copies element values.
For int[][], shallow clone shares inner row arrays; demonstrate with one changed element.
Know object array clones share referenced objects, not deep-copy the objects.
Reimplement Arrays.copyOf using a loop to understand semantics.
Use Arrays.sort(a) and know it mutates input in place.
Know Arrays.parallelSort as a parallel alternative, not always faster for small data.
Use Arrays.binarySearch only when the searched region is sorted appropriately.
Know binarySearch missing index is encoded as -(insertionPoint)-1, not always -1.
Use Arrays.equals for same-type 1D element comparison and deepEquals for nested.
Use Arrays.mismatch to locate first differing index; returns -1 when contents match.
Know Arrays.compare lexicographically compares two arrays and Java version availability.
Know Arrays.setAll / parallelSetAll to compute index-based new element values.
Check API overloads for primitive arrays vs object arrays.
Understand Arrays.asList(new String[]{"a","b"}) yields a fixed-size list backed by the object array.
Understand changing list.set changes backing array but list.add/remove is unsupported.
Know Arrays.asList(int[]) makes List<int[]> with one array element, not List<Integer>.
Use Arrays.stream(int[]).boxed().collect(Collectors.toList()) for mutable primitive-to-wrapper lists.
Distinguish char, String and char[]; know a String is immutable.
Use s.length(), s.charAt(i), s.substring(from,to), s.indexOf(substr).
Use s.equals(other) for text equality rather than ==; know null-safety.
Use Objects.equals(a,b) when either reference may be null.
Know s.toCharArray(), new String(chars), String.valueOf(number).
Use Character.isLetterOrDigit, isDigit, toLowerCase for filtered comparisons.
Know s.split(regex) is regex-based; regex metacharacters matter.
Use trim versus strip at a high level; avoid rebuilding string in loops accidentally.
Understand Unicode/UTF-16 caveat: charAt uses UTF-16 code units, not always whole characters.
Use StringBuilder append, setCharAt, reverse, toString and capacity basics.
Know + concatenation in a repeated loop may cause extra work.
Compare two strings character-by-character and handle different lengths.
Explain palindrome via two pointers and case/punctuation normalization.
Know substring vs subsequence vs prefix vs suffix.
Implement frequency array for lowercase ASCII-style constraints; guard input alphabet assumptions.
Know String.compareTo lexicographical comparison (not equivalent to equals).
Know array is fixed-size; ArrayList is a dynamically resizable list built around an array internally.
Distinguish List<Integer> (interface type) from ArrayList<Integer> (concrete implementation).
Understand primitive int vs wrapper Integer and boolean vs Boolean.
Read List<Boolean> result = new ArrayList<>(); left is interface, right constructs implementation.
Use add(value), get(index), set(index,value), remove(index), size(), isEmpty(), contains().
Know get(index) is O(1) and end add is amortized O(1); inserting near front is O(n).
Use result.add(candies[i] + extra >= max) because comparison evaluates to a boolean first.
Know auto-boxing converts primitive boolean to Boolean object for List<Boolean>.
Distinguish result[i] = x (array) from result.add(x) (list).
Avoid using List<List<Integer>> until a single List makes sense.
Know ArrayList cannot take primitive generics e.g. ArrayList<int> is invalid.
Know array of List objects has null default slots until initialized.
Integer[] boxed = {1,2}; new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(boxed)) produces growable list.
Convert List<Integer> to int[] using stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray().
Convert int[] to List<Integer> using Arrays.stream(a).boxed().collect(Collectors.toList()).
Know list.toArray(new Integer[0]) gives object array; not int[].
Avoid conflating List.of(...) with mutable ArrayList; know Java versions may differ.
Understand nested List<List<Integer>> row.get(col), row lists can vary in size.
Distinguish set (unique values) from list (ordered positions) and map (key to value).
Instantiate Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>(); know import java.util.*.
Use add, contains, remove, size; understand add returns boolean.
Explain expected O(1) membership vs scanning array O(n); worst-case caveat.
Explain iteration order is not guaranteed by HashSet.
Understand duplicate detection pattern as you traverse elements.
Know custom object keys rely on compatible equals and hashCode.
Instantiate Map<Integer,Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();.
Use get, put, containsKey, getOrDefault, remove, keySet, values, entrySet.
Compute freq.put(x, freq.getOrDefault(x,0)+1).
Explain map key versus associated value and overwrite semantics for duplicate keys.
Implement Two Sum using complement target - x, checking before insertion where appropriate.
Build map of character frequencies for strings; compare counts.
Explain hash collisions, load factor and resize only at a conceptual level.
Know HashMap permits one null key (unlike several concurrent variants).
Distinguish HashMap from TreeMap (sorted keys) and LinkedHashMap (iteration behavior).
Understand Collection, List, Set, Queue, Deque and Map at a practical level.
ArrayDeque for stack: push, pop, peek; for queue: offer, poll, peek.
Explain why Stack class is usually less preferred than ArrayDeque for new code.
PriorityQueue<Integer> is min-heap by default; peek/poll behavior.
Use Comparator.reverseOrder to create max-heap PriorityQueue where valid.
Understand PriorityQueue offers O(log n) insertion and polling, O(1) peek.
Know ArrayList random access O(1), linked list random access O(n).
Distinguish HashSet, TreeSet and LinkedHashSet on ordering and complexity.
Know Collections.sort(list), reverse(list), min/max(list) and Arrays.sort(array).
Use Comparator.comparingInt and custom comparators for pairs/objects.
Explain why modifying a collection while iterating may cause ConcurrentModificationException.
Know mutable vs immutable vs fixed-size collection families.
Use stack for nested parentheses and monotonic neighbors.
Use queue for BFS; know visit once with a visited set.
Use heap for top K and streaming tasks.
Use list for ordered growing output and map for key-based lookup.
Use HashMap with ArrayDeque for graph adjacency and BFS.
Know when sorted collections justify O(log n) operations.
Explain stream as a pipeline over values, not a replacement collection.
Know Arrays.stream(int[]) returns IntStream; Arrays.stream(Integer[]) returns Stream<Integer>.
Know IntStream.sum, max, min, average; max/min return OptionalInt, average OptionalDouble.
Understand OptionalInt.getAsInt can throw if empty; use orElse or guard based on constraints.
Know map, filter, sorted, distinct, boxed, toArray, count, collect.
Identify intermediate vs terminal operations and pipeline lazy evaluation.
Learn Stream.of, list.stream and IntStream.range(0,n).
Avoid streams where an explicit loop is clearer for a coding interview.
Know side effects in parallel streams can create race conditions.
Know stream() cannot be reused after a terminal operation.
Arrays.stream(intArray).boxed().toList() yields List<Integer> where supported; toList may be unmodifiable.
Collectors.toList does not guarantee a particular mutability contract; new ArrayList<>(...) for a mutable result.
list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray() yields int[].
Use Arrays.asList(String[]) for backed fixed-size list; not with primitive arrays as element expansion.
Use String.join, String.valueOf, StringBuilder.toString at the right step.
Distinguish map transformations from filter tests and reduce accumulation.
Learn method references Integer::intValue, but be able to rewrite as x -> x.intValue().
Arrays of objects contain reference slots; new String[3] initially holds nulls.
Assignment Person b = a copies a reference; mutating through b changes shared object state.
Understand final reference prevents reassignment, not necessarily mutation of object.
Use == for primitive values; == on objects checks reference identity.
String.equals compares content; Objects.equals(a,b) handles nulls.
Arrays.equals compares one level of array contents; deepEquals handles nested arrays recursively.
Know Arrays.equals(new int[]{1},new int[]{1}) true but (a == b) false for separate arrays.
Recognize array covariance: Object[] x = new String[2]; storing Integer triggers ArrayStoreException.
Explain shallow vs deep copy and when immutable String makes sharing safe.
Define class, field, constructor, object and method; distinguish instance vs static.
Explain encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism with small real examples.
Prefer composition when inheritance is not a real is-a relationship.
Differentiate interface from abstract class at basic level.
Know equals/hashCode contract when classes act as HashMap keys.
Know access modifiers public, protected, package-private, private.
Explain immutability and defensive copies in APIs.
Understand simple SOLID ideas: single responsibility, dependency inversion, interface segregation.
Know checked vs unchecked exceptions, try/catch/finally and meaningful error messages.
Define input size n (or m and n for matrices); make explicit which variable scales.
Rank O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n), O(n!).
Count the work of one loop, nested loops, triangular loops, binary loops and separate loops.
Explain O(n+m) vs O(n*m); don't always collapse independent inputs.
Derive binary search O(log n) from repeated halving.
Know sorting complexity O(n log n) for comparison-based efficient sorts.
Recognize worst-case vs average-case hash lookups.
Understand amortized cost: append to dynamically resized arrays.
Distinguish total space, auxiliary space and recursion stack usage.
Know that result array of length n requires O(n) output storage even if extra working variables are O(1).
Analyze nested recursion, branching factor, depth and memoization states.
Recognize that slicing/copying inside recursion can increase complexity.
Explain brute force first, then demonstrate why a faster approach works.
Use loop invariant: what remains true before and after every iteration?
Distinguish preconditions, postconditions and termination arguments.
Write counterexamples for greedy ideas and invalid binary-search predicates.
Know when sortedness is essential for two-pointer or binary-search algorithms.
Explain trade-offs: speed vs memory, simplicity vs optimization, precompute vs query.
Recognize input constraints that require better than quadratic algorithms.
Linear traversal: visit each element once, track a running answer.
Accumulation: sum, product, prefix max, count matches.
Running best: update min/max correctly, especially for negative-only input.
Two-pass processing: compute a reference value first, then evaluate each item.
Output-index construction: write to new array indexes i, i+n and arithmetic mappings.
In-place compaction: write pointer tracks retained prefix.
Reversal/rotation: swap or reverse segments, handle n=0 where applicable.
Counting consecutive runs: reset state on interruptions, take maximum.
Build output from mapping or transformed values.
Strings: match chars, prefixes, suffixes, case folding, substring boundaries.
Matrix: row/column traversal, diagonals, transpose, boundary checks.
Sort-and-scan: distinguish sorted vs unsorted before selecting algorithm.
Test empty and length one if allowed; duplicate and all-same arrays.
Test all negative values when max/min initialization matters.
Check in-place required versus allowed new output array.
Explain O(n) loop plus O(n) output, and whether input mutation is acceptable.
Set membership for duplicates and visited items.
Complement HashMap for target sum; check previous values and retain index.
Map value frequency for each int or character.
Compare count maps for anagrams or multiset equality.
Group by canonical key: sorted string or character-count encoding.
Find first unique element with count + second pass.
Prefix sum to frequency map for subarray sums.
Track earliest/latest index with map for distance conditions.
Recognize hashing only supports expected O(1), not always guaranteed.
Use different data structures for bounded alphabet vs arbitrary strings.
Explain HashMap values changing on duplicate keys.
Distinguish counting duplicates from returning distinct results.
If order/rank is needed, consider sorting or TreeMap.
If keys are small integers, a counting array may be simpler and lower overhead.
Watch memory when input keys are very large or all unique.
Opposite-end pointers on sorted input; move the side that can improve target.
Palindrome validation while ignoring case or non-alphanumerics.
Read/write pointers for removing or compacting values in place.
Slow/fast runners to find linked-list midpoint and cycles.
Two-array merge with pointer into each sequence.
Sort then two-pointer for 3Sum, skip duplicate candidate values.
Squares of sorted array: compare absolute ends and fill from back.
Container With Most Water: why shorter wall pointer moves.
Sliding window is related but has distinct validity-maintenance invariant.
Subsequence scan: move pointer in short string only on match.
Deduplicate sorted array while preserving a valid prefix.
Partitioning: know when original order need not be maintained.
Explain why advancing this pointer cannot skip a better candidate.
Test duplicate values, no solution, equal ends, one-element inputs as allowed.
Distinguish in-place O(1) auxiliary space vs sorted preparation cost.
Recognize exact-length subarray/substring requirement.
Maintain sum by adding entering and subtracting leaving value.
Compute window length as right-left+1 for inclusive endpoints.
Use array count or HashMap for fixed-window character counts.
Know monotonic deque for sliding window maximum as a later extension.
Identify feasibility predicate that allows left to move while right grows.
Maintain count of distinct chars, duplicates, or budget remaining.
Grow right; while invalid, shrink left and update state.
Update best length at the correct point, after validity established.
Understand at-most-K distinct and exact-K via subtraction of two at-most counts.
Minimum-size window vs maximum-size window logic; don't mix them.
Recognize when negative numbers invalidate simple sum-based shrink logic.
Use mutable maps without leaving zero counts as phantom distinct keys.
Test repeated chars, full window, empty answers and single-char cases.
Create prefix[0]=0 and prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+a[i].
Query sum for interval [l,r] as prefix[r+1]-prefix[l].
Know alternative n-length prefix convention and off-by-one risk.
Maintain cumulative frequency or parity states instead of raw sum.
Pivot index via running left and total-right-left.
Prefix products and suffix products for division-free product except self.
Prefix HashMap: sum(curr)-sum(prev)=target, count prior occurrences.
2D prefix sum using inclusion-exclusion formula; draw the four rectangles.
Difference array for efficient range increment updates; reconstruct by prefix summing.
Know when preprocessing wins for many repeated queries.
Handling negative numbers, zeros, long sums; choose long if sum might overflow.
Define inclusive/exclusive bounds before writing queries.
Know output storage complexity versus O(1) working state.
Understand sortedness precondition for finding exact match.
Use left, right, mid; avoid overflow with left+(right-left)/2.
Understand inclusive [left,right] and half-open [left,right) variants.
Shrink bounds every iteration and avoid infinite loops.
Return found index or -1; search insert position variant.
Find first occurrence/last occurrence with boundary templates.
Distinguish lower bound and upper bound semantics.
Handle empty arrays, duplicates, all values smaller/larger than target.
Define a monotonic feasible(predicate) function.
Find minimum feasible or maximum feasible parameter.
Explain why every feasible value on one side makes binary search legal.
Compute count with ceiling division carefully.
Analyze O(log range × cost(feasible)) runtime.
Avoid relying blindly on Arrays.binarySearch if answer is not exact membership.
Know comparison vs noncomparison sorts and stability.
Trace insertion sort and selection sort; show why quadratic.
Implement merge sort divide/merge and analyze O(n log n) time O(n) extra space.
Trace quicksort partition and average vs worst case.
Know heap sort at conceptual level and heaps as priority queues.
Know Java Arrays.sort for primitive arrays vs custom object comparators.
Design comparators correctly; don't subtract ints when overflow possible.
Sort interval arrays by start or end as required by greedy proof.
Use sorting to expose duplicates, close values, or opposing pointer opportunities.
Know quickselect for kth-smallest, average O(n), worst O(n^2).
Distinguish sorting entire array from heap top-K when K much smaller than n.
State whether sort mutates input and changes original order.
Explain when adding O(n log n) sort still beats O(n^2) brute force.
Recognize stable sort requirement only when the prompt needs it.

sections.title: Stacks / queues / monotonic structures
sections.sourceTitle: Pattern lab 08: Stacks / queues / monotonic structures

skills.text: Implement stack with ArrayDeque; know push/pop/peek and empty guard.
Match opening/closing delimiters while scanning string.
Use stack for expression parsing, reverse-polish notation and decoding strings.
Use queue for BFS with offer/poll and maintain visited state.
Understand why queue order gives shortest path in unweighted graphs.
Understand monotonic increasing vs decreasing stacks; distinguish stored values vs indexes.
Find next greater element / stock span / daily temperature using monotonic stack.
Analyze each index pushed/popped once -> O(n) for many monotonic stack algorithms.
Use deque for monotonic sliding-window max as stretch.
Design Min Stack with additional minimum history.
Check stack empty before pop/peek, nested brackets, unmatched closing, zero-length input.
Explain direction of scan and when answer is known.
Draw a singly linked node value + next reference.
Explain head, tail, null terminator, and why random access is O(n).
Create a ListNode in Java and manually connect 3 nodes.
Reverse list with prev/current/next pointers; trace one mutation at a time.
Use dummy head to avoid special first-element insertion/deletion logic.
Merge two sorted lists with tail pointer.
Remove nth node from end via fast/slow separation.
Find middle with slow/fast; detect cycle with Floyd pointers.
Know length counts versus two-pointer alternatives.
Recognize reversing in groups and palindrome list as later variations.
Understand immutable next? no: node.next is mutable unless design prevents it.
Know basic doubly linked list prev/next for LRU cache design.
Avoid losing remaining list by changing next before saving it.
Test one node, two nodes, null head and repeated values.
Explain O(1) extra space for iterative reverse and O(n) recursion stack for recursive reverse.
Distinguish root, parent, child, leaf, depth, height and subtree.
Binary tree vs binary search tree vs complete tree vs balanced tree.
Draw DFS preorder, inorder, postorder and explain visit order.
Implement recursive traversal returning data or computing an aggregate.
Write correct base case for null node.
Track recursion call stack space proportional to tree height.
Implement BFS level-order traversal with queue and levels.
Max depth, min depth and symmetry patterns.
BST ordering invariant and search/insert behavior; skewed worst case O(n).
Validate BST using allowable ranges, not just parent comparisons.
Lowest common ancestor in arbitrary binary tree vs BST.
Construct tree from traversal information under relevant uniqueness assumptions.
Serialize/deserialize with null markers to preserve structure.
Tree diameter and path sums with postorder return values.
Balanced tree idea: height and update invariants; no need to memorize full AVL rotation code at first.
N-ary traversal and trie are related tree variants.
Explain min heap complete-tree shape and parent/child array index mapping.
Know insert, peek, extract operations and O(log n) vs O(1) complexity.
Use Java PriorityQueue and comparator for max heap.
Solve top-K with min heap of size K; compare sorting O(n log n).
Understand k-way merge using heap entries from each sorted list.
Median streaming using two heaps (max-heap lower half, min-heap upper half).
Understand heapify O(n) vs repeated insert O(n log n).
Know that a heap is not a globally sorted array.
Draw nodes as characters and edges, marking end-of-word separately.
Implement insert, exact search and startsWith.
Explain alphabet array children vs HashMap children tradeoffs.
Know time O(length of key) for lookup rather than full dictionary scan.
Recognize word search and autocomplete prefixes as uses.
Distinguish vertices, edges, directed/undirected, cyclic/acyclic, weighted/unweighted.
Build adjacency list (Map<Integer,List<Integer>> or List<List<Integer>>).
Understand adjacency matrix space O(V^2) and lookup tradeoff.
Recognize grid as implicit graph; four-direction coordinates, bounds checks.
Use a visited boolean array/set, including when to mark visited in BFS.
Trace BFS level by level and DFS recursion/iterative stack.
Analyze O(V+E) traversal for adjacency lists, O(m*n) grid scan/traversal.
Find connected components and number of islands.
Cycle detection in undirected graph via parent; directed via three-color state.
Bipartite graph checking using two-color BFS/DFS.
Multi-source BFS for nearest exit/rotting oranges.
Shortest unweighted path via BFS and parent reconstruction.
Topological sorting via Kahn indegrees or DFS ordering.
Distinguish trees as connected acyclic graphs.
Know state can include position + extra dimensions (keys, visited mask, remaining resources).
Avoid stack overflow on very deep recursion by using iterative stack/queue if needed.
Check start/end obstacles, disconnected graphs, isolated nodes.
Represent each node with parent and rank/size arrays.
Understand find with path compression and union by size/rank.
Recognize connectivity queries, grouping and cycle checks.
Know near-constant amortized DSU operation and inverse Ackermann idea.
Dijkstra for nonnegative edge weights with min heap.
Differentiate BFS shortest unweighted from weighted shortest-path search.
Understand visited/finalized distances and stale heap entries.
Recognize Bellman-Ford for negative edges and negative-cycle detection conceptually.
Know Floyd-Warshall all-pairs and O(V^3) when needed.
Minimum spanning tree purpose; compare Kruskal sorting edges + DSU with Prim heap growth.
A* as an optional informed search; admissible heuristic intuition.
State when a shortest-path tree is not the same as MST.
Convert strange narrative into nodes, edges, state and transitions.
Identify time/memory costs based on generated state count.
Explain dependency edges for course schedule or build order.
Identify base case, recursive case, parameters and progress toward termination.
Explain stack frames, call order, and return-value contracts.
Compare recursion vs explicit stack and tail-call limitations in Java.
Use choose → explore → undo for mutable shared path/backtracking.
Generate subsets with include/exclude branching.
Generate permutations using used flags or swaps.
Generate combinations with increasing start index to avoid duplicates.
Generate balanced parentheses with open/close constraints.
Word Search: visited cell, boundary, restore on backtrack.
N-Queens: row-by-row placement and invalid diagonals.
Prune impossible partial states early; document why pruning is sound.
Estimate search tree size and complexity beyond simple O(n).
Know copying path into results (new ArrayList<>(path)) avoids later aliasing.
Forgetting to undo mutation or to copy result path.
Reusing one visited array incorrectly across independent search branches.
Starting branching from wrong index in combinations vs permutations.
Define objective and candidate local greedy decision.
Give counterexample when a plausible greedy fails.
Use exchange argument or stay-ahead proof when possible.
Sort intervals by start for merging, by end for maximizing compatible selections.
Merge overlapping intervals correctly including boundaries touching.
Meeting Rooms capacity / sweep line event counting.
Jump Game reachability via farthest reachable index.
Gas Station concept: maintain total balance and reset start on deficit.
Task scheduling using frequency or heap; recognize when greediness works.
Greedy vs dynamic programming: local independent choice vs interdependent states.
Test equal endpoints, contained intervals, negative values, disconnected ranges.
Sort cost dominates O(n log n), then linear scan.
Know when to keep original indices before sorting.
Identify repeated overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
Define state as a precise question; e.g., dp[i] = best answer for prefix ending at i.
Define transition from smaller solved states and explain why exhaustive over choices.
Pick base cases correctly before coding.
Implement top-down memoization with sentinel/cached state.
Implement bottom-up tabulation in dependency order.
Space optimization with rolling variables when only nearby states needed.
House Robber: choose take vs skip; handle small n.
Coin Change: impossible sentinel and unbounded coin repetitions.
Climbing Stairs: linear recurrence with O(1) optimization.
Grid paths DP and obstacle handling.
Longest increasing subsequence O(n^2) then patience sorting O(n log n) idea.
Longest common subsequence and edit distance 2D state.
0/1 knapsack vs unbounded knapsack; loop direction matters in 1D space.
Partition equal subset sum and target sum transformations.
Decode Ways and string-position DP.
Stock buy/sell state machine as advanced extension.
Interval DP and bitmask DP are optional later-specialized study.
Count number of states times work per state.
Explain recursion memoization stack and table space.
Use small hand-drawn state table before code; test first/last row and empty prefix.

sections.title: Math, bits & optional specialties
sections.sourceTitle: Pattern lab 17: Math, bits & optional specialties

skills.text: GCD Euclidean algorithm, LCM via division to minimize overflow.
Modulo arithmetic, frequency remainders and safe normalization.
Prime testing up to sqrt(n), Sieve of Eratosthenes as needed.
Basic permutations/combinations, n choose k, elementary probability.
Arithmetic series formula and counting invariant; know overflow.
Binary representations and bit indexing.
Bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts; differentiate signed >>> from >>.
Odd/even bit check, set/clear/test bit, XOR to find unique value.
Bitmask subsets for small n; state compression concept.
Know integer overflow when computing mid or products.
Segment tree range queries and updates; lazy propagation.
Fenwick/Binary Indexed Tree prefix sums.
Tries with failure links / KMP and rolling hash string matching.
Strongly connected components (Tarjan/Kosaraju), bridges/articulation points.
Computational geometry orientation/cross products, sweeping.
Network flow and min-cut; advanced DP optimizations.
Bloom filters, probabilistic structures and distributed primitives as specialty knowledge.
Explain program vs process vs thread; separate process memory and shared thread memory.
Know context switching, CPU scheduling, blocking versus nonblocking I/O.
Understand heap vs stack memory, object allocation and garbage collection at a high level.
Explain virtual memory, pages, address spaces and page faults at introductory depth.
Know synchronization: mutex, monitor, semaphore, volatile, atomic operations.
Recognize race condition using read-modify-write example.
